Temple blocks are struck idiophones, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.243, derived from the East Asian wooden fish or wooden bell and common in religious ritual. The instrument is a hollowed, carved wooden body with a large slot; the traditional form is slightly round and bell-like, and modern ones are mostly rectangular. They are usually played in sets of four or more to obtain different pitches, and are also called tuning blocks. In Western music they can be traced to early jazz drummers using them as an exotic colour, and later they came into orchestral use.
寺廟木魚源自東亞木魚或木製鐘，用於宗教儀式。傳統形制略呈鐘形，現代多為矩形，常以: Temple blocks derive from the East Asian wooden fish or wooden bell and are used in religious ritual. The traditional form is slightly bell-shaped, the modern mostly rectangular, and they are often grouped in fours or more, a set of five being tuned mostly to a pentatonic scale, with chromatic and diatonic sets also made; in sets they are also called tuned wooden fish. After they reached the West, early jazz drummers used them as an exotic instrument, and later they entered the orchestra; the Latin Percussion company has also brought out a plastic version, the granite blocks.

The source also records a newer version made by the Latin Percussion company, called the granite blocks, in which plastic replaces wood. 站於琴前，雙手持棒敲擊琴鍵中央。手持樂器本體，透過敲擊、搖晃、刮奏或撥彈等方式使: Stand in front of the instrument and strike the centre of the bars with a stick in each hand. Hold the body of the instrument and set it vibrating by striking, shaking, scraping or plucking it; different points and different amounts of force give different timbres. In practice, first confirm the correct holding position and master the basic way of sounding the instrument, then work on rhythm patterns and melody. Strike the surface with the fingers or a stick and let it rebound naturally from the bounce, keeping the wrist relaxed.
